quizName: DMV Practice Test #6 50 Questions • Passing Score 40

questions.question: When approaching a bump or pothole, you should rise slightly off your seat:

options.text: So you can jump off the motorcycle if needed.
So your legs can absorb the shock.
So other drivers can see you better.
So you can see the bump or pothole better.

questions.correctAnswerText: So your legs can absorb the shock.
questions.explanation: When riding over bumps or potholes, rising off your seat lets your body absorb the impact. This reduces the force of the impact and helps keep you on the motorcycle.

questions.question: In a no passing zone:

options.text: A motorcycle can still pass another vehicle.
A motorcycle cannot pass another vehicle.
A motorcycle can pass if it finishes before another vehicle approaches.
A motorcycle can pass on the shoulder.

questions.correctAnswerText: A motorcycle cannot pass another vehicle.
questions.explanation: Passing is not allowed in no passing zones. You also cannot pass by riding off the main road.

questions.question: When carrying a passenger in a sidecar, you should:

options.text: Start slowing down sooner than usual.
Start slowing down later than usual.
Brake harder than usual to stop quickly.
Brake gently than usual to avoid overworking the brakes.

questions.correctAnswerText: Start slowing down sooner than usual.
questions.explanation: The extra weight of a passenger in a sidecar changes how your motorcycle handles. Your motorcycle will need more space to stop.

questions.question: Braking in a turn is:

options.text: Easier than braking on a straight road.
Harder than braking on a straight road.
Done safely by using only the front brake.
Done safely by using only the rear brake.

questions.correctAnswerText: Harder than braking on a straight road.
questions.explanation: Braking in a turn is harder than braking on a straight road. You can use both brakes in a turn, but you must know the correct technique and be very careful.

questions.question: When checking tire pressure:

options.text: Looking at the tire is a good method.
Use a tire gauge.
Squeeze the tire to check it.
Compare the tire height to another tire.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use a tire gauge.
questions.explanation: Use a tire gauge to check tire pressure before every ride. A tire that is not fully inflated may still look fine, so looking at it is not enough.

questions.question: Your riding clothes should protect you from all of the following, except:

options.text: Sunburn.
Windburn.
Chapped lips.
Dehydration.

questions.correctAnswerText: Chapped lips.
questions.explanation: Your riding clothes should protect you from sunburn, windburn, rain, dehydration, cold, and motorcycle parts. Your clothes should also help protect you if you crash.

questions.question: When another vehicle is passing you, all of the following are hazards, except:

options.text: Extended mirrors.
Objects thrown from the other vehicle.
Wind gusts from the other vehicle.
Headlights.

questions.correctAnswerText: Headlights.
questions.explanation: When being passed, watch out for the vehicle's mirrors hitting you. Also be aware of wind gusts from the passing vehicle and objects that passengers might throw.

questions.question: Alcohol impairs your riding ability:

options.text: Well below the legal limit.
Only at the legal limit.
Just above the legal limit.
Well above the legal limit.

questions.correctAnswerText: Well below the legal limit.
questions.explanation: Never ride after drinking any amount of alcohol. Your riding skills become impaired well before you reach the legal limit.

questions.question: Flash your brake light most importantly when:

options.text: Passing another vehicle.
You need to slow down suddenly.
A stop sign is ahead.
Your turn signals do not work.

questions.correctAnswerText: You need to slow down suddenly.
questions.explanation: A motorcycle's brake light is smaller and less noticeable than a car's brake lights. Flashing your brake light helps other drivers notice when you are slowing down quickly.

questions.question: As your motorcycle's weight shifts forward while braking, you:

options.text: Can squeeze the front brake harder.
Should use less pressure on the front brake.
Can squeeze the rear brake harder.
Lose traction.

questions.correctAnswerText: Can squeeze the front brake harder.
questions.explanation: As your weight shifts forward while braking, the front wheel has more grip. This means you can apply the front brake with more force.

questions.question: A motorcyclist should always look ahead at the road for:

options.text: Road conditions.
Traffic conditions.
Ways to escape danger.
All of the above.

questions.correctAnswerText: All of the above.
questions.explanation: Always look ahead to stay alert. Watch for changes in traffic, hazards on the road, and places you can safely go if danger appears. Be ready to react quickly.

questions.question: Riding in cold weather for long periods can cause all of these, except:

options.text: Fatigue.
Hypothermia.
Severe chills.
Hot flashes.

questions.correctAnswerText: Hot flashes.
questions.explanation: Cold weather riding can cause severe chills, fatigue, and hypothermia. Always wear proper clothing to protect yourself from the cold.

questions.question: During a normal turn:

options.text: The motorcycle and rider should lean together.
The motorcycle and rider should lean in opposite directions.
The motorcycle should lean, but the rider should not.
The rider should lean, but the motorcycle should not.

questions.correctAnswerText: The motorcycle and rider should lean together.
questions.explanation: During normal turns, the motorcycle and rider lean together at the same angle. In slow, tight turns, only the motorcycle leans while the rider stays upright.

questions.question: When riding in a group, inexperienced riders should position themselves:

options.text: In the front of the group.
Just behind the leader.
Close to the back of the group.
At the very end of the group.

questions.correctAnswerText: Just behind the leader.
questions.explanation: Less experienced riders should ride just behind the leader. This way, they won't fall behind the group. Experienced riders behind them can also watch and help them.

questions.question: In a slow, tight turn, the rider should:

options.text: Keep their body upright while the motorcycle leans.
Lean at the same angle as the motorcycle.
Lean in the opposite direction of the motorcycle and turn.
Keep the motorcycle upright while their body leans.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep their body upright while the motorcycle leans.
questions.explanation: For normal turns, lean with your motorcycle. For slow, tight turns, keep your body upright while the motorcycle leans.

questions.question: A rectangular sign may be a:

options.text: School crossing sign.
Railroad crossing sign.
Stop sign.
Speed limit sign.

questions.correctAnswerText: Speed limit sign.
questions.explanation: Rectangular signs with white backgrounds and black letters show road rules, like speed limits. You must follow the rules on these signs.

questions.question: Where is the engine cut-off switch usually located?

options.text: Near the left handgrip
Near the right handgrip
Near the left footrest
Near the right footrest

questions.correctAnswerText: Near the right handgrip
questions.explanation: The engine cut-off switch is located next to the right handgrip. Learn where all your motorcycle controls are before you ride.

questions.question: For motorcycle safety, you should:

options.text: Assume everything on your motorcycle works properly.
Check your motorcycle before every ride.
Check your motorcycle once a month.
Check your motorcycle twice a week.

questions.correctAnswerText: Check your motorcycle before every ride.
questions.explanation: Small problems on a motorcycle are more dangerous than on a car. Always check your motorcycle thoroughly before each ride.

questions.question: To be seen in the rearview mirror of a driver ahead, you should:

options.text: Ride in the center of the lane.
Ride in the left side of the lane.
Ride in the right side of the lane.
Ride in a weaving pattern.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the center of the lane.
questions.explanation: Position yourself in the center of your lane behind the car. This puts you in their rearview mirror. Drivers look in their rearview mirrors much more than side mirrors.

questions.question: When riding near stopped or slow cars, a motorcyclist should:

options.text: Pull over and wait for traffic to move.
Ride on the shoulder to pass quickly.
Weave between cars to pass quickly.
Not weave between the cars.

questions.correctAnswerText: Not weave between the cars.
questions.explanation: Weaving between stopped or slow cars is dangerous. Car doors may open or cars may suddenly move into traffic. You won't have room to escape safely. Never ride on road shoulders because other drivers don't expect you there.

questions.question: When riding a motorcycle at night instead of during the day, which of the following should you NOT do?

options.text: Ride more slowly.
Leave more space between your motorcycle and other vehicles.
Use your high beam when possible.
Tailgate other vehicles.

questions.correctAnswerText: Tailgate other vehicles.
questions.explanation: To avoid crashes at night, slow down and increase your following distance. Use the headlights of vehicles ahead to see farther down the road. Change your lane position as needed, especially at night.

questions.question: When passing parked cars, a motorcycle operator should be ready for:

options.text: Empty parking spaces.
A car to suddenly pull out of a parking space into traffic.
Parking meters.
Other drivers to see you and stay out of your way.

questions.correctAnswerText: A car to suddenly pull out of a parking space into traffic.
questions.explanation: When passing parked cars, a parked car may suddenly pull into traffic. Ride on the left side of your lane when passing parked cars on your right. This creates more space between you and any hazards.

questions.question: If a small animal enters your lane while you are riding in traffic, you should:

options.text: Swerve into other lanes to avoid hitting the animal.
Change lanes as quickly as possible.
Stay in your lane.
Flash your lights to scare the animal away.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stay in your lane.
questions.explanation: Avoid hitting animals when possible. But if you are in traffic, stay in your lane. Swerving into another lane could cause you to hit another vehicle. Hitting a small animal is safer than hitting another car.

questions.question: To work well, an eye or face shield should have all of these features, except:

options.text: Be free of scratches.
Resist being penetrated.
Fasten securely.
Be airtight.

questions.correctAnswerText: Be airtight.
questions.explanation: Good eye protection and face shields must be free of scratches, resist penetration, have clear side vision, fasten securely, allow air to pass through, and fit over eyeglasses or sunglasses.

questions.question: If a dog is chasing you, you should:

options.text: Kick it away.
Stop until it loses interest.
Swerve around it.
Approach it slowly, then speed up.

questions.correctAnswerText: Approach it slowly, then speed up.
questions.explanation: Dogs often chase motorcycles. If chased by a dog, downshift and ride slowly toward it. Then accelerate and leave it behind.

questions.question: If a dog is chasing your motorcycle, you should:

options.text: Swerve around it.
Stop until it loses interest.
Ride alongside it.
Approach it slowly, then speed up.

questions.correctAnswerText: Approach it slowly, then speed up.
questions.explanation: If chased by a dog, downshift and ride slowly toward it. Then accelerate and leave it behind.

questions.question: When carrying a load in a sidecar, you should:

options.text: Let the load move freely.
Secure the load so it does not shift.
Place the load unsecured in the seat.
Secure the load near the front of the sidecar.

questions.correctAnswerText: Secure the load so it does not shift.
questions.explanation: Secure loads in a sidecar so they do not shift and affect handling. Place loads toward the rear of the sidecar to prevent the nose from tipping during sharp left turns.

questions.question: What type of sign is yellow with black lettering or symbols?

options.text: Warning
Service
Regulatory
Speed limit

questions.correctAnswerText: Warning
questions.explanation: Warning signs are yellow with black lettering or symbols. They warn drivers about upcoming road conditions.

questions.question: When slowing or stopping, you should use both brakes:

options.text: Only if the pavement is wet.
Not very often.
Only when riding in the city.
Every time.

questions.correctAnswerText: Every time.
questions.explanation: Using both the front and rear brakes gives you the strongest stopping power. Use both brakes every time you slow down or stop.

questions.question: When passing parked cars on your right with no oncoming traffic on your left, you should:

options.text: Stay on the right side of your lane.
Stay on the left side of your lane.
Look to your left frequently.
Use your rearview mirrors more often than usual.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stay on the left side of your lane.
questions.explanation: When passing parked cars, stay on the side of your lane away from the cars. This protects you from car doors opening or people stepping out. If oncoming traffic is present, stay in the center of your lane.

questions.question: As a beginning rider, what should you do when following another vehicle?

options.text: Keep at least a four-second distance behind the vehicle.
Get as close to the other vehicle as possible.
Do not worry about following distance.
Always ride on the left side of the lane so the driver can see you.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep at least a four-second distance behind the vehicle.
questions.explanation: Beginning riders should keep at least a four-second distance behind other vehicles. Increase this distance if road or weather conditions are not ideal.

questions.question: What is the best protection for a motorcycle rider?

options.text: Keep space between your motorcycle and other vehicles.
Wear a good leather jacket.
Wear sturdy boots.
Know motorcycle laws well.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep space between your motorcycle and other vehicles.
questions.explanation: The best way to avoid hitting other vehicles is to stay far away from them. This gives you time to react if another driver makes a mistake. Wearing proper safety gear is also important.

questions.question: When you borrow a motorcycle, what should you do?

options.text: Do not check the tire pressure.
Assume it will handle like your own bike.
Trust that the owner checked the brakes for you.
Leave extra space between you and other vehicles to give yourself more time to react.

questions.correctAnswerText: Leave extra space between you and other vehicles to give yourself more time to react.
questions.explanation: Check a borrowed motorcycle the same way you would check your own before riding. Ride carefully on an unfamiliar motorcycle and leave extra space for stopping.

questions.question: What do you NOT need to check before every ride?

options.text: The spokes.
The tire tread.
The lights.
The seat fabric.

questions.correctAnswerText: The seat fabric.
questions.explanation: Before every ride, check that the rims and spokes are not bent or damaged, check your tire condition and tread, and check all lights. You do not need to check the seat fabric.

questions.question: How often should you do a complete check of your motorcycle?

options.text: Before every ride.
Once a week.
Once a month.
Once a year.

questions.correctAnswerText: Before every ride.
questions.explanation: Motorcycles need more frequent checks than cars. Always do a complete check before each ride.

questions.question: The center of a lane often has an oily strip. When is this area safe for motorcycles?

options.text: Never.
Usually safe, but not when the road is wet.
Usually safe, but not on sunny days.
Always safe in all weather.

questions.correctAnswerText: Usually safe, but not when the road is wet.
questions.explanation: Oil from cars collects in a strip in the center of lanes. When the road is dry, this area usually gives enough traction for safe riding. When wet, avoid it. The strip is usually only two feet wide, so you can often ride around it and still stay in the center part of the lane.

questions.question: If you cannot avoid a slippery surface, what should you do?

options.text: Speed up and lean the motorcycle.
Speed up and keep the motorcycle upright.
Slow down and lean the motorcycle.
Slow down and keep the motorcycle upright.

questions.correctAnswerText: Slow down and keep the motorcycle upright.
questions.explanation: If you cannot avoid a slippery surface, keep your motorcycle upright and go as slowly as possible.

questions.question: When riding with a passenger, what should you NOT tell them to do?

options.text: Get on after the engine starts.
Sit as far forward as possible without crowding you.
Hold firmly onto your waist, hips, or belt.
Talk whenever they want.

questions.correctAnswerText: Talk whenever they want.
questions.explanation: Passengers should not talk unnecessarily or move around, so you can focus on riding. Passengers should get on only after the engine starts, sit forward without crowding you, and hold your waist, hips, or belt firmly.

questions.question: When approaching a blind intersection with a stop sign, what should you do?

options.text: Stop at the sign and proceed through the intersection.
Ignore the stop sign and move forward to see better.
Stop at the sign, then move forward slowly to look both ways before proceeding.
Do not stop and go through the intersection.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stop at the sign, then move forward slowly to look both ways before proceeding.
questions.explanation: Stop where the stop sign indicates. Then slowly move forward and stop again just before entering the cross traffic area. Lean forward to look around buildings, parked cars, or bushes. Make sure your front wheel does not enter the crossroad while you are looking.

questions.question: What is true about intersections for motorcycle riders?

options.text: They are safe because there is a lot of traffic.
They are dangerous spots for riders.
They are confusing.
They are safer than open roads.

questions.correctAnswerText: They are dangerous spots for riders.
questions.explanation: Intersections are dangerous because they create the most conflict between motorcyclists and other drivers.

questions.question: At night, should your following distance be longer or shorter than during the day?

options.text: You should stay farther back from the vehicle ahead at night.
You should stay closer to the vehicle ahead at night.
You should keep the same distance at night as during the day.
Following distance does not matter.

questions.correctAnswerText: You should stay farther back from the vehicle ahead at night.
questions.explanation: At night, it is hard to judge how far away other vehicles are. You cannot see shadows or light changes as clearly. Stay farther back at night than you do during the day.

questions.question: To stop quickly, what should you do?

options.text: Use only the front brake.
Use only the rear brake.
Use the front brake first, then the rear brake.
Use both brakes at the same time.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use both brakes at the same time.
questions.explanation: To stop quickly, apply both brakes together.

questions.question: When should a motorcyclist shift gears?

options.text: While turning.
Before turning.
By changing power suddenly during a turn.
While using the brakes throughout the turn.

questions.correctAnswerText: Before turning.
questions.explanation: Shift gears before you enter a turn.

questions.question: What helps other drivers see you at an intersection?

options.text: Making eye contact with other drivers.
Riding with your headlight on.
Reducing the space between you and other vehicles.
Weaving side to side as you ride.

questions.correctAnswerText: Riding with your headlight on.
questions.explanation: Keep your headlight on at intersections so other drivers can see you. Ride in a position that makes it easy for oncoming traffic to see you. Keep space around you to escape if needed. Never assume a driver sees you, even if you make eye contact.

questions.question: When riding over rough surfaces, how should you hold the handgrips?

options.text: Loosely to let the motorcycle move.
Firmly to keep control.
With lots of throttle to get over the rough surface.
Without a helmet so it does not cover your face.

questions.correctAnswerText: Firmly to keep control.
questions.explanation: On rough surfaces, grip the handlebars firmly. This keeps your motorcycle going in the right direction.

questions.question: If your throttle gets stuck, what should you do?

options.text: Jump off the motorcycle.
Apply the brakes.
Twist the throttle back and forth several times.
Do not try to twist the throttle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Twist the throttle back and forth several times.
questions.explanation: If the throttle is stuck, twist it back and forth several times. If it does not free up, use the engine kill switch and pull in the clutch at the same time.

questions.question: How should a motorcyclist's following distance change?

options.text: It should always be the same.
It should change based on riding conditions.
It is not needed in most situations.
It should be small to keep traffic moving.

questions.correctAnswerText: It should change based on riding conditions.
questions.explanation: Increase your following distance if your motorcycle takes longer to stop, if the road is slippery, if you cannot see past the vehicle ahead, or if traffic is heavy.

questions.question: How often does a motorcycle need maintenance compared to a car?

options.text: Less often than a car.
More often than a car.
Only a mechanic should do pre-ride checks.
Only a dealer can service it.

questions.correctAnswerText: More often than a car.
questions.explanation: Small problems on a motorcycle are more serious than on a car. Check your motorcycle more often. Do a full check before every ride.

questions.question: What helps you avoid crashes?

options.text: Using your turn signals when you plan to change lanes.
Following other drivers very closely.
Looking only 15 feet ahead of your motorcycle.
Not using your headlight during the day.

questions.correctAnswerText: Using your turn signals when you plan to change lanes.
questions.explanation: To avoid crashes, be visible, signal your moves, keep space around you, look 12 seconds ahead, spot hazards early, and be ready for changes.

questions.question: How much of a motorcycle's stopping power comes from the front brake?

options.text: About one-quarter
About one-half
About three-quarters
All of it

questions.correctAnswerText: About three-quarters
questions.explanation: The front brake is more powerful than the rear brake. It provides about three-quarters of the total stopping power.
